notes: Article 8 family life appeal; IAT reasons held inadequate and remitted; facts and authorities are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker: Article 8 family life reasons
key_facts: Mr Senthuran, a Sri Lankan Tamil, arrived in the UK aged 17 in July 1997 and lived continuously with siblings who had refugee status or pending appeals.
The Home Office took over four years to refuse his asylum claim in October 2001; an adjudicator dismissed asylum but allowed an Article 8 appeal.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal reversed the Article 8 decision, holding that adult sibling relationships did not establish family life or that removal would be proportionate.
The Court of Appeal held the IAT failed adequately to reason on highly relevant facts including long delay and continuous cohabitation since arrival as a minor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against an IAT decision allowing the Secretary of State's appeal from an immigration adjudicator's Article 8 determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT determination set aside and Secretary of State's appeal remitted to the IAT for rehearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where Article 8 turns on whether family life exists between adult siblings, adjudicators and the IAT must identify the nature of the asserted family life and explain why Article 8 is or is not engaged; reciting facts in the history is not enough if those facts are not incorporated into the reasoning, and the IAT's reliance on Advic and Salad did not justify ignoring the appellant's continuous residence with siblings since age 17 and the Home Office's four-year delay.
legal_issues: Whether Article 8 was engaged by family life between adult siblings living together
Whether removal would be disproportionate given delay and settled private life
Whether the IAT gave adequate reasons for reversing the adjudicator
Application of Advic v United Kingdom and Salad to sibling cases
linked_authorities: Advic v United Kingdom (20 EHRR CD125)
Salad [2002] UKIAT 06698

confidence.notes: Outcome, Article 8 reasoning critique, and remittal order are explicit. Appellant did not appear and merits on remittal were expressly reserved.

notes: Shaken-baby conviction quashed for summing-up defects; unsafe verdict analysis and no-retrial decision are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe GBH conviction where two possible perpetrators
key_facts: K was convicted of inflicting grievous bodily harm and cruelty to a two-year-old child after the mother left the house on 27 January 2003.
Medical evidence indicated a very serious shaking incident that morning; the defence case was that the mother or a prior injury could have caused the harm.
The Recorder allowed cross-examination on the appellant's prior marriage but directed the jury it was of little significance.
Critical prosecution evidence from the mother and ambulance worker Lawrence Bigg was omitted from the summing-up and the Recorder failed to return to summarise the appellant's evidence as promised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge following jury trial at Cardiff Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Convictions on counts 3 and 4 quashed as unsafe; appeal allowed and no retrial ordered given time already served in custody.
enrichment.ratio: Where there are two possible perpetrators of injury to a child and the evidence does not conclusively identify which adult caused it, the summing-up must carefully identify the evidence, warn the jury about the interest of the only other possible perpetrator, and fairly summarise all relevant evidence; omissions of key prosecution evidence and failure to complete the defence summary render the conviction unsafe.
legal_issues: Safety of conviction where mother and appellant were both possible perpetrators
Adequacy of summing-up on counts 2 and 3 after acquittal on count 1
Whether cross-examination on marriage to the Registrar was permissible
Whether a retrial should be ordered
linked_authorities: R v Lloyd
R v Vye

confidence.notes: Grounds for quashing and retrial refusal are fully reasoned. Character direction criticism was expressly not decisive.

notes: Complex insurance jurisdiction dispute; Colman J's analysis of proper law, service-of-suit clause and forum is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: BP open-cover insurers: jurisdiction and proper law upheld

statutes_considered.title: Rome Convention on the Law Applicable to Contractual Obligations
Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Law Applicable to Contracts of Insurance) Regulations 2001

key_facts: BP sought to serve AIG and AEGIS in New York and New Jersey in a dispute over validity of declarations under a global construction all-risks open cover.
Moore-Bick J had granted permission to serve out; the insurers applied to set aside that order.
General Condition 16 gave BP discretion to select English or USA law; a binder condition allowed service of suit in the UK or USA at the insured's discretion.
AIG and AEGIS had commenced overlapping proceedings in New York before BP's English claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside an order granting permission to serve English proceedings on foreign insurers outside the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; English jurisdiction upheld on both governing-law and jurisdiction-clause grounds and discretion exercised in favour of England.
enrichment.ratio: A unilateral option in General Condition 16 to select English or USA law, when exercised, validly substituted English law as the proper law of contracts under the open cover; the service-of-suit clause conferred a jurisdictional option dovetailled with the law option; where parties agreed to English jurisdiction, commencing parallel proceedings elsewhere on forum conveniens grounds alone is oppressive absent exceptional unforeseen circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether General Condition 16 was an effective floating or deferred choice-of-law clause
Whether the service-of-suit clause was an enforceable jurisdiction clause
Whether BP validly exercised its options
Forum non conveniens and parallel New York proceedings
linked_authorities: Armar Shipping v Caisse Algerienne d'Assurance [1981] 1 WLR 207
Du Pont v Agnew [1987] 2 Lloyd's Rep 585
BP plc v G E Frankona Reinsurance Ltd [2003] 1 Lloyd's Rep 537
Sabah Shipyard (Pakistan) Ltd v Islamic Republic of Pakistan [2003] 2 Lloyd's Rep 571
Ace Insurance SA-NV v Zurich Insurance Co [2001] 1 Lloyd's Rep 618

notes: Planning enforcement costs JR; unreasonable failure to enquire before stop notice; quashing and costs assessment clear.

enrichment.short_title: Planning enforcement costs after Bude temporary shop dispute
key_facts: Mr Cobbledick erected a temporary timber shop unit at 14 Belle Vue, Bude to trade while refurbishing the premises for his oceancrafts business.
North Cornwall District Council issued enforcement and stop notices in August 2001 without contacting him; he successfully appealed the change-of-use notice.
The Secretary of State initially issued a minded decision to award full costs against the Council but later refused costs.
Sullivan J had previously dismissed the Council's challenge to the inspector's appeal decision in the underlying enforcement case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to award costs following a successful planning enforcement appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Secretary of State's costs decision quashed; claimant's judicial review costs summarily assessed at £9,500.
enrichment.ratio: A local planning authority acts unreasonably in serving a broad change-of-use enforcement notice backed by a stop notice without making elementary enquiries about the temporary structure's purpose and duration; where the owner would have removed the eyesore by mid-August, such enforcement was unnecessary, ineffective and excessive, and the Secretary of State erred in treating stop-notice compensation as a separate matter that justified refusing appeal costs.
legal_issues: Whether the Council behaved unreasonably in issuing the enforcement notice
Whether failure to consult before enforcement justified a costs award
Application of PPG 18 guidance on enforcement against small businesses
Whether judicial review costs were proportionate
linked_authorities: North Cornwall District Council v Secretary of State for Transport, Local Government and the Regions [2003] EWHC 2318 Admin
R (London Borough of Ealing) v Secretary of State for Environment [1999] EWHC Admin 345

confidence.notes: Core unreasonableness finding and quashing order are robust and clearly explained. Costs quantum involved summary assessment adjustments.

notes: Urgent stay application refused; uninhabitable fire-damaged flat and hopeless appeal grounds clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Tenant refused stay after fire made flat uninhabitable
key_facts: Mr Rhodes held a tenancy of a top-floor flat at 80c Lancaster Road from Kensington Housing Trust.
After a fire on 27 March 2004 the Trust sought an order requiring him to vacate temporarily for repairs and offered alternative accommodation.
HHJ Lindsay ordered Mr Rhodes to give up possession for four months from 23 April 2004; a stay pending appeal was discharged by Grigson J on 13 May 2004.
Surveyors gave uncontradicted expert evidence that the flat was unsafe and uninhabitable until extensive repair works were completed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent application for permission to appeal and reinstatement of a stay of execution pending appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; permission to appeal effectively denied as grounds were hopeless and Grigson J's discharge of the stay upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where independent surveyor evidence establishes that premises are unsafe and uninhabitable after fire damage, a judge is entitled and bound to order temporary vacation for repairs; it would be absurd simultaneously to require reinstatement of electricity while ordering the tenant out, and a tenant's covenant to allow access carries an implied obligation to vacate where works cannot safely proceed with occupation.
legal_issues: Whether the flat was uninhabitable after the fire
Whether the tenant should remain pending appeal
Whether the Trust was entitled to require temporary vacation under the tenancy
Whether electricity reinstatement should have been ordered

confidence.notes: Short interlocutory judgment with straightforward factual and legal conclusions. No linked authorities were cited.

notes: Security for costs after Nasser; residence and enforcement-burden analysis leading to £100,000 order is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Security for costs against Hong Kong oil-exploration claimant
key_facts: Texuna, a Hong Kong company, claimed over US$121 million against Cairn Energy after an unsuccessful Caspian oil-exploration bid.
Cairn applied for £500,000 security for costs under CPR 25.13 on grounds of foreign residence and inability to pay.
Texuna contended it was resident in England because directors Mr and Mrs Agarwal lived here, but had paid no UK corporation tax.
The claim had been dramatically amended upward after the original US$550,000 claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for security for costs in commercial proceedings, adjourned once to address Nasser principles on quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Security ordered in the sum of £100,000 rather than the £500,000 sought.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 25.13(2)(a) Texuna was resident in Hong Kong for security purposes; inability to pay under paragraph (2)(c) was not established on the Unisoft test, but following Nasser v United Bank of Kuwait discretion could still be exercised where enforcement abroad would involve extra cost and delay; for Hong Kong the appropriate security is tailored to the additional enforcement burden rather than full estimated costs, here assessed at about £50,000 plus £50,000 for risk of more complex enforcement.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant was resident out of the jurisdiction
Whether there was reason to believe the claimant would be unable to pay costs
Effect of Nasser on discretion and quantum of security
Relevance of location of assets for enforcement risk
index_terms: Aims Asset Management v Kazakhstan Investment Fund
linked_authorities: Nasser v United Bank of Kuwait [2001] EWCA Civ 556
Re Unisoft Group Ltd (No 2) [1993] BCLC 532
In re Little Olympian Ltd [1995] 1 WLR 560
Hammond Suddard v Agrichem [2001] EWCA Civ 2065

confidence.notes: Residence, inability-to-pay and Nasser quantum conclusions are explicit. Some asset-location authority conflicts were noted but not finally resolved beyond this case.

notes: Winchester boundary dispute; transfer construction, boundary agreement and estoppel conclusions are detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Winchester boundary dispute over steep garden bank
key_facts: Professor and Mrs Chadwick bought Park House from Abbotswood Properties after a 1996 Winchester development; the Hausers owned neighbouring Greenwood House below a four-metre bank.
The transfer plan placed the boundary at the top of the bank; the Chadwicks later claimed the bank formed part of their title.
Meetings in June and August 1996 led to a fence on the bank top, a supplemental agreement and correspondence suggesting the Chadwicks did not want to own the bank.
A separate strip or tongue beside the access road was also in dispute with Rectory Pump Ltd.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim for declaration of boundary ownership and related rectification issues.
enrichment.outcome: Claim largely failed; bank held to belong to the Hausers/Greenwood side; narrow eastern yellow-strip boundary declared for Chadwicks but ransom-strip claim by access road rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Construing the 1996 transfer objectively, the reasonable lay purchaser would not have acquired the steep bank; the Land Registry plan, landscaping plan and retained-land definition placed the boundary at the fence on the bank top; oral meetings and the supplemental agreement constituted a boundary agreement and proprietary estoppel preventing the Chadwicks from asserting ownership of the bank.
legal_issues: Construction of transfer parcels and filed plan
Effect of the general boundaries rule
Whether there was an oral boundary agreement
Proprietary estoppel arising from fence and landscaping works
Ownership of access-road verge strips
index_terms: Alan Wibberley Building Ltd v Insley
linked_authorities: Alan Wibberley Building Ltd v Insley [1999] 1 WLR 894
Lee v Barrey [1957] Ch 251
Freeguard v Rogers [1999] 1 WLR 375
Joyce v Rigolli [2004] EWCA Civ 79
Taylor Fashions Ltd v Liverpool Victoria Trustees Co Ltd [1982] QB 133

notes: Very long share-forfeiture trial; main voidability and locus standi holdings are clear but many subsidiary issues and costs remain unresolved.

enrichment.short_title: Minority shareholder challenges forfeiture after unpaid call
key_facts: Mr Hunter, a minority shareholder in Senate group companies, had his shares forfeited for non-payment of a £300 call after acrimonious breakdown with the majority led by Mr Cookson and Mr and Mrs Tippins.
Directors of three subsidiaries resolved in November 2002 to forfeit and transfer the shares to group holding company SVSP after two Table A call notices.
The claimant sought to impugn forfeiture primarily to regain standing to bring unfair prejudice petitions under section 459.
The judge rejected a conspiracy/set-up case but found directors treated forfeiture as inevitable and failed to consider realistic alternatives.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim to set aside share forfeiture and rectify registers; locus standi and Wednesbury-style director decision-making in issue.
enrichment.outcome: Forfeiture decisions held voidable and to be set aside; claimant has locus standi; order form and costs left to further submissions.
enrichment.ratio: Directors who forfeit shares under Table A must exercise a genuine discretion and consider material alternatives to forfeiture; a decision made on the mistaken belief that forfeiture was the only available course after non-payment, without considering realistic alternatives, is voidable where it might or would have been different had proper consideration been given; a shareholder may sue in his own name to set aside forfeiture of his shares as an infringement of individual shareholder rights.
legal_issues: Whether forfeiture was for an improper purpose
Whether directors failed to consider alternatives to forfeiture
Void or voidable effect of flawed director decisions
Claimant's locus standi outside Foss v Harbottle
Validity of call notices and deemed receipt
linked_authorities: Howard Smith Ltd v Ampol Petroleum Ltd [1974] AC 821
Sweney v Smith (1857) 3 K & J 529
Provident International Corporation v International Leasing Corporation [1969] 1 NSWLR 424
Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223
Abacus Trust Co (Isle of Man) v Barr [2003] Ch 409

notes: Attorney General's reference on unduly lenient s18 sentence; increase to 3.5 years with double jeopardy adjustment is clear.

enrichment.short_title: AG reference: bottle-glass wounding sentence increased
key_facts: A 23-year-old offender was convicted after trial of wounding with intent following a carnival fracas at Maidenhead in June 2002.
He returned ten minutes after an earlier fight, broke a bottle and jabbed it into the victim's face causing ten lacerations requiring 17 stitches.
The sentencing judge imposed 30 months' imprisonment; aggravating features included retribution, deliberate arming and facial injury.
Mitigation included prior racist abuse directed at the offender's party, good character and that the offender acted out of character.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 alleging an unduly lenient sentence after jury trial at Reading Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; sentence increased from 30 months to three and a half years' imprisonment after double jeopardy adjustment.
enrichment.ratio: For section 18 wounding with intent involving a deliberately broken bottle thrust into the face in retribution after a public disturbance, a 30-month sentence after trial failed adequately to reflect gravity, deterrence and public concern; allowing for double jeopardy, a sentence of at least four and a half years would have been expected at first instance.
legal_issues: Whether 30 months was unduly lenient for section 18 wounding with intent
Weight of retribution, arming and facial injury
Effect of racist provocation and good character
Application of double jeopardy on reference
linked_authorities: Attorney-General Reference No 25 of 2002 [2003] 1 Cr App R(S) 28
Attorney-General's Reference No 24 of 1998 [1999] 1 Cr App R(S) 278
Attorney-General Reference No 41 of 1994 16 Cr App R(S) 792
Attorney-General's Reference No 9 of 1995 [1996] 1 Cr App R(S) 116

confidence.notes: Aggravating and mitigating features and substituted sentence are stated explicitly with citation of prior AG references.

notes: Football reinsurance misrepresentation appeal; valued policy materiality and warranty analysis are detailed and outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Football relegation reinsurance avoided for misrepresentation
key_facts: Spanish insurers Vitalicio fronted cover for Atletico Madrid against economic loss from relegation linked to television rights owed to Audiovisual Sport.
London-market reinsurers led by Banco Vitalicio accepted facultative reinsurance described as indemnifying net ascertained loss of contracted television rights up to Pts 2.9bn.
The underlying policy was in fact a valued policy for Pts 2.9bn; Atletico was relegated in May 2000 and insurers paid Audiovisual Pts 2.7bn.

Reinsurers refused payment and successfully argued the misdescription was material because the Club's economic loss could realistically be less than Pts 2.9bn once a Pts 500m European qualification refund obligation was accounted for.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Andrew Smith J's judgment rescinding the reinsurance and declaring reinsurers discharged from liability.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; reinsurers entitled to avoid for material misrepresentation and breach of description warranty.
enrichment.ratio: Where reinsurance is proportional and the interest clause describes an indemnity for net ascertained loss but the underlying policy is a valued policy, the misdescription is material to a prudent underwriter if there is a realistic possibility the net ascertained loss on relegation would be less than the valued sum; calculating economic loss requires comparing 2000/01 first-division earnings net of the contingent Pts 500m repayment obligation with second-division earnings, and that contingent obligation was capable of valuation.
legal_issues: Materiality of misdescribing a valued policy as an indemnity policy
Whether the interest clause was a warranty
Construction of the full reinsurance clause
How Audiovisual contract terms affected ascertained loss
linked_authorities: HIH Casualty and General Insurance Ltd v New Hampshire Insurance Co [2001] EWCA Civ 735
Toomey v Eagle Star [1994] 2 Lloyd's Rep 516
Vesta v Butcher [1989] AC 852
Barnard v Faber [1893] QB 340

confidence.notes: Misrepresentation holding and warranty conclusion are central and fully reasoned. Full reinsurance clause cross-appeal was left undecided.
